feynman_topics.evidence: Every living thing is built from cells, and every cell runs the same basic plan: a membrane-wrapped interior where organelles divide the work. The nucleus stores the DNA — the instruction set — while ribosomes build proteins from those instructions. Mitochondria release energy from food molecules, the cytoskeleton gives the cell its shape and moves materials around, and the cytoplasm is the gel where most chemistry happens. Plant cells add a rigid wall and chloroplasts; animal cells do without both. Structure is not decoration — each part exists because it does a job the whole cell depends on.

The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer: two sheets of fat-like molecules with their water-loving heads facing out and water-fearing tails facing in. That arrangement makes the membrane selectively permeable — small uncharged molecules slip through, while ions and large molecules need help from embedded proteins. Channel proteins form pores, carrier proteins shuttle specific cargo, and receptor proteins pass signals inward. Cholesterol tucked between the phospholipids keeps the membrane fluid but stable. The membrane is therefore both a wall and a customs post: it decides what enters, what leaves, and what the cell hears about the world outside.

Check yourself: What does the cell membrane do? Controls what enters and leaves the cell.

Photosynthesis is how plants, algae, and some bacteria turn light energy into stored chemical energy. Inside chloroplasts, pigments — chiefly chlorophyll — absorb mostly blue and red light, which is why leaves look green. In the light-dependent reactions, water is split, releasing oxygen, and its energy is captured in the carriers ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle then spends those carriers to build sugars from carbon dioxide, no light required. The balance sheet: carbon dioxide plus water becomes glucose plus oxygen — and nearly every food chain on Earth runs on that captured sunlight.

Cellular respiration releases the energy photosynthesis stored. It runs in three acts. Glycolysis, in the cytoplasm, splits one glucose into two pyruvate molecules and nets a small payment of ATP — no oxygen needed. The Krebs cycle, in the mitochondrial matrix, strips the pyruvate down to carbon dioxide and loads energy carriers. The electron transport chain then spends those carriers, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor, forming water and driving the bulk of ATP production. Total yield: roughly thirty ATP per glucose — the cell's spendable currency, earned by controlled burning instead of fire.

Before a cell can divide, it must copy its DNA — all of it, once, accurately. The double helix unzips as helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, and each exposed strand becomes a template. DNA polymerase builds the new strand by matching free nucleotides to the template — A with T, C with G — but it can only build in one direction, so one strand is made continuously and the other in short Okazaki fragments that ligase later seals. The result is semi-conservative: each daughter molecule keeps one original strand and one new one, and proofreading keeps errors near one in a billion bases.

Mitosis divides one nucleus into two genetically identical nuclei. In prophase the copied chromosomes condense and the spindle — a scaffold of microtubules — begins to form. Metaphase lines the chromosomes along the cell's equator, each attached to spindle fibers from both poles, a checkpoint that ensures every daughter gets a full set. Anaphase pulls the sister chromatids apart to opposite poles. Telophase wraps each set in a new nuclear envelope, and cytokinesis then splits the cytoplasm. One cell in, two identical cells out — the mechanism behind growth, repair, and asexual reproduction.

feynman_topics.evidence: A sample only speaks for the population it was fairly drawn from. Volunteers differ from the people who stay silent, customers who answer a survey differ from those who ignore it, and a poll of whoever walked past differs from the town. That gap between who got asked and who the claim is about is bias, and no amount of extra data repairs it — a bigger biased sample is just a more confident wrong answer. Random selection is the repair: when every member of the population has a known, non-zero chance of being picked, the differences average out instead of piling up.

Before any analysis, name what was actually measured. A variable records one attribute per case: categorical variables sort cases into groups (major, blood type, yes-or-no), while quantitative variables carry numbers where arithmetic means something (height, reaction time, income). The same question can hide different variables — 'hours studied' measured by self-report is not the variable a timestamp log measures. Units and definitions are part of the data: a temperature in Celsius, a score out of 40, and a count of errors behave differently in every later calculation.

Probability assigns every event a number between 0 and 1, and the whole sample space gets exactly 1. Three rules do most of the work. The complement rule: an event fails to happen with probability 1 minus the chance it happens. The addition rule: disjoint events add — the chance of either is the sum of their chances. The multiplication rule: independent events multiply — the chance of both is the product. Most probability errors are rule errors: adding events that overlap, or multiplying events that are not independent, like two draws from the same small deck without replacement.

Check yourself: What is the complement rule for the probability that an event does NOT happen? One minus the probability that it does happen: P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

A random variable turns an uncertain outcome into a number. Roll two dice and the count of sixes is a random variable; so is the sum, the time until the next bus, or whether tomorrow's trial succeeds. Discrete variables take countable values, each with its own probability; continuous ones spread probability over intervals, described by a density curve where area is probability. Two summaries carry most of the story: the mean, the long-run average the values settle toward, and the standard deviation, the typical distance from that mean.

The normal curve is a symmetric, bell-shaped density fixed by two numbers: its mean, which centers it, and its standard deviation, which sets its spread. Its great convenience is the empirical rule — about 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two, and 99.7% within three. Standardizing converts any normal value to a z-score, the count of standard deviations from the mean, so one table serves every normal distribution. Many natural measurements and nearly all sample averages lean toward this shape, which is why it anchors the course.

A statistic computed from a sample — a mean, a proportion — is itself a random variable, with its own distribution: the sampling distribution. Draw many samples of the same size and the sample means pile into a shape that is narrower than the population's and, by the central limit theorem, close to normal for large samples whatever the population looked like. Its standard deviation, the standard error, shrinks like 1 over the square root of the sample size: quadrupling the sample halves the wobble. This is the bridge from one sample to an honest claim about a population.

The Calvin cycle then spends those carriers to build sugars from carbon dioxide, no light required. The balance sheet: carbon dioxide plus water becomes glucose plus oxygen — and nearly every food chain on Earth runs on that captured sunlight.
sections.title: photosynthesis

sections.text: Cellular respiration releases the energy photosynthesis stored. It runs in three acts. Glycolysis, in the cytoplasm, splits one glucose into two pyruvate molecules and nets a small payment of ATP — no oxygen needed. The Krebs cycle, in the mitochondrial matrix, strips the pyruvate down to carbon dioxide and loads energy carriers. The electron transport chain then spends those carriers, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor, forming water and driving the bulk of ATP production. Total yield: roughly thirty ATP per glucose — the cell's spendable currency, earned by controlled burning instead of fire.
sections.title: respiration

sections.text: Before a cell can divide, it must copy its DNA — all of it, once, accurately. The double helix unzips as helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, and each exposed strand becomes a template. DNA polymerase builds the new strand by matching free nucleotides to the template — A with T, C with G — but it can only build in one direction, so one strand is made continuously and the other in short Okazaki fragments that ligase later seals. The result is semi-conservative: each daughter molecule keeps one original strand and one new one, and proofreading keeps errors near one in a billion bases.
sections.title: DNA replication

sections.text: Mitosis divides one nucleus into two genetically identical nuclei. In prophase the copied chromosomes condense and the spindle — a scaffold of microtubules — begins to form. Metaphase lines the chromosomes along the cell's equator, each attached to spindle fibers from both poles, a checkpoint that ensures every daughter gets a full set. Anaphase pulls the sister chromatids apart to opposite poles. Telophase wraps each set in a new nuclear envelope, and cytokinesis then splits the cytoplasm. One cell in, two identical cells out — the mechanism behind growth, repair, and asexual reproduction.
